prompt: For years I dreaded the idea of having kids, and now that I have them I feel completely differently. Write a personal essay about that change: what I got wrong beforehand, what I got right, and how honest I can be about it given that parenthood probably rewires your brain.
honest question for parents who used to be really driven: did having kids make you less productive or less ambitious?
Write a short essay on how people actually lose money once they have it, and whether the same pattern applies to how we waste time.
I just came into a decent chunk of money and I'm paranoid about blowing it. How do rich people actually end up losing their fortunes?

You've spent years doing office hours with early-stage startups. Write an essay about the question you find more useful than "how can this company make more money": how could it become more powerful? Cover the different forms that takes and what limits it.
Is "create more value than you capture" just a nice-sounding idealistic slogan, or is it actually a good way to get rich?
We're a B2B startup and my cofounder wants to target big companies because that's where the money is. Isn't selling to tiny early-stage startups a waste of time since they have no budget?

If a university genuinely wanted more of its students to go on to start successful startups, what should it do, and what should it avoid? Write it up as an essay, from the perspective of someone who funds those students right after they graduate.
My university has almost no startup culture. What's the most effective thing we could do to get more students to actually consider starting a company?
Why do startup investors care so much about side projects students built on their own, rather than grades?
Our school runs a business plan competition every year to encourage entrepreneurship. Is that actually useful preparation for starting a startup?

You've been invited to speak to a student debating society full of future politicians, and a prominent politician recently claimed nobody can earn a billion dollars without cheating. Write the talk: explain how people actually become billionaires through startups, and what someone young would need to do to get there.
I'm a college student who wants to start a company. Should I build something for a market I've researched, or something I want myself?
Do you basically have to exploit people to get really rich from a startup?

Politicians keep talking about a "small" 1% wealth tax. How does a wealth tax rate compare to an income tax rate? Write a short, clear piece explaining how to convert between the two and why it matters.

An essay has to tell readers something they don't already know. Write a short reflective essay on the different reasons readers might not know something, and what that implies about who an essayist ends up writing for.

I want a long essay on how the Swiss luxury watch industry survived the quartz crisis by turning itself into a business of brand, and what that history reveals about the relationship between branding, design, and quality.
What actually happened to the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s "quartz crisis", and how did the survivors come out of it?

Is there any real connection between writing that sounds good and writing whose ideas are right? It seems like those should be independent, like a car's speed and its paint color. Write an essay working out whether they are.
what does it actually mean for prose to have good rhythm? is it like meter in poetry or something else?

Write an essay taking on the big childlike question: what should one do with one's life? Not a self-help listicle, an actual attempt at an answer from first principles, and consider why older traditions answered it the way they did.
Now that AI can write for people at school and at work, what happens to the ability to write? Give me a short, punchy essay with a prediction and say whether it matters.

"Follow your passion" gets argued about endlessly. I'd like an essay that actually maps out when you should work on what interests you most and when you shouldn't, rather than giving a yes-or-no answer.
I'm in college and torn between a field I find really interesting and one that pays a lot better. Neither pull is clearly stronger. How do I break the tie?

You run a startup accelerator. Lately a lot of successful founders have told you that the standard advice for scaling a company, hire good people and give them room, nearly wrecked their businesses. Write an essay about why that advice might be wrong for founders and what the alternative could look like.

Write an essay on persistence versus obstinacy. Is there a real behavioral difference between the stubbornness that leads to success and the kind that leads nowhere, or do we just label people after the fact depending on whether they turned out to be right?
is there actually a difference between being persistent and just being stubborn? or do we only call it persistence when it works out

You co-founded Y Combinator and funded Reddit in the very first batch. Write a personal piece about Reddit's founders and how the company got started, and what it says about the match between founders and the companies they build.

I've been asked to give a talk to a room of 14 and 15 year olds about what they should be doing now if they might want to start a big tech company someday. Write the talk. Keep it concrete and in language teenagers will follow.
I'm 15 and I think I want to start a tech company eventually. How do I get good at technology, and how do I even pick which technology to learn? I'm already taking CS at school.
What would the best possible essay be like? Take that question seriously and follow it wherever it leads, including into how essays actually get written.

We were all raised on 'you get out what you put in.' I'm increasingly convinced that's false and that rewards for performance are wildly nonlinear in most areas that matter. Write an essay on where these outsized returns come from and what an ambitious person should do about it.
Is there any general rule for finding work where the payoff grows superlinearly instead of just adding up?
If you had to boil down how to do really great work into a short recipe, what would it be?
Short essay idea: if we met intelligent aliens, which truths beyond math and physics would we probably share with them, and why might asking that be a useful exercise for philosophy?
Write an essay about what happens to your ideas when you try to put them into words. Is it possible to have fully formed ideas about something you've never written about?
does writing something up actually change what you think, or is it just recording ideas you already had?
Is there really such a thing as good taste, or is it all just preference? I'm giving a talk to a student debating society and want a short, rigorous argument for one side. Write it as an essay.
Plenty of very smart people never discover anything new. Write an essay on the gap between intelligence and having new ideas, and what else goes into the latter.
I grew up thinking being really smart was the most important thing. Is it actually what matters?

My kid came home excited to keep working on a story nobody assigned him. It got me thinking about how different that kind of work is from schoolwork or a job. Write an essay about working on projects of your own: what makes them different, where the boundary lies, and how adults can keep doing it.
As a kid I started projects constantly without thinking twice. As an adult I barely start any side projects. Why is it so much harder now and what can I do about it?
What actually makes a piece of work feel like 'your own' project rather than something you're just doing because you were told to?

People picture nerds as meek, but some of the most competitive people I know are nerds. Write an essay about this fierce type of nerd: what they're like, why it works for them, and some advice for young people who recognize themselves in it.
Write an essay on how we should react when a serious expert proposes an idea that sounds absurd, and why so many people are quick to dismiss new ideas.
A respected expert in their field just proposed something that sounds completely crazy to me. Should I just write it off?
Debates about the death penalty usually focus on morality and deterrence. Write a short, forceful essay (as of around 2021) arguing that the real issue is something more practical.
Compare the Forbes 400 lists from the early 1980s and from 2020. How has the way people get very rich in America changed, and why? Write it up as an essay, written from the vantage point of 2021.
why is it easier to start a startup now than a generation ago, and how does that affect how rich founders get?
Write a short blog post on why you try to write in plain words and simple sentences.

You and your partner have been judging startup founders for years, and you have a private vocabulary for the qualities you look for. Write an essay about one of those words: earnestness. Why would an old-fashioned virtue like that matter so much in a place like Silicon Valley?
What does it actually mean to call someone earnest? And is it a strength or a weakness? It always sounds slightly uncool to me.

Politicians keep saying the only way to become a billionaire is by exploiting people. You spent years at Y Combinator trying to pick the founders who would get enormously rich. Write an essay that uses what you actually looked for in YC interviews to answer that claim, and give founders honest advice on how to do well in the interview along the way.

I have my YC interview next week. What should I do if they ask me something I don't know the answer to, or start grilling me about what could go wrong and who my competitors are? My instinct is to make everything sound airtight.

Airbnb just went public, and you funded them back in 2008 when nobody else would. Write a short piece for future founders about what was special about the Airbnb founders and how they got the company off the ground during Y Combinator.

Write an essay on independent-mindedness: which kinds of work require thinking differently from your peers, whether people can tell where they fall on that spectrum, and whether it's possible to make yourself more independent-minded.

I'm trying to choose a career. Does it matter whether I'm the kind of person who naturally thinks differently from everyone around me, or is that just a personality thing that doesn't affect which job I should pick?
can you actually make yourself more independent-minded, or are you just born that way? what helps?
Is there any way to become more curious as an adult? I feel like I've lost a lot of it.

We're usually taught that an essay should be persuasive. I'd like a more ambitious standard. Write an essay on what it means for writing to be genuinely useful, how a writer can actually achieve that, what it costs you, and how someone should start.
What actually makes a piece of nonfiction writing good, as opposed to just persuasive or correct? Can you break it down?
How do you revise an essay? How many times do you reread before you're done, and how do you know when it's ready to publish?
My writing teacher says never to start a sentence with "I think" because hedging makes writing weak. Is that right?

Founders are often caught off guard by the attention they get as their companies grow, including people who seem obsessed with hating them. Write an essay about haters: what they are, where they come from, and how someone who becomes famous should deal with them.
Write a short essay on political moderates. Is being a moderate just cowardice or fence-sitting, or is there more than one way to end up in the middle?

Write an essay about what school really teaches people, beyond the subject matter of any class, and how that lesson follows them into adult life and work. You've spent years advising young startup founders fresh out of college, so draw on what you saw there.
why are school tests so easy to game? it seems like everyone who gets good grades knows how to study for the test rather than learn the material
Is there a quick way to tell whether a test or evaluation actually measures what it claims to, or whether it can be gamed?
You grew up in Pittsburgh and now live in Silicon Valley, and you've been asked to give a talk in Pittsburgh. Write the talk: what would it actually take for Pittsburgh to become a startup hub?
If a research university like CMU wanted to help its city become a startup hub, what should it actually do? Entrepreneurship centers? Something else?
Everyone says life is short. Is it actually, or is that just a complaint about it being finite? And if it is short, what should that change about how we live? Write an essay on this.
Random thought: is life actually short, or would we say that no matter how long we lived?
What kinds of things do you think life is too short for, and how do you actually get them out of your life?
Why is it so hard to reduce economic inequality? It seems like policy should be able to fix it.
Is there any way for an outsider to tell whether a selection process (hiring, admissions, VC funding) is biased, without access to data on who applied? Write a short piece explaining how.
Can you detect bias in who gets selected for something if you only know about the people who got picked, not the whole applicant pool?
A founder tells you he's worried he's too soft-hearted to succeed and gives too much away for free. Write a short essay on whether startup founders can afford to be nice.
Should a US startup that doesn't own the .com of its name change its name? Write a short, opinionated essay for founders.
Write a short essay about Ron Conway, and what his career suggests about whether being genuinely good pays off for investors.
Isn't it enough to just seem like a good person in business? Why would anyone bother actually being good if appearances do the job?
Someone from a big company's corporate development team wants to meet with our young, fast-growing startup. Write an essay for founders in this position: should they take the meeting?
corp dev at a big tech company reached out wanting to 'chat'. we're not looking to sell but it can't hurt to hear them out, right?
Tech companies keep lobbying for easier immigration for programmers, and critics say we should just train more Americans instead. Write a short, punchy essay taking a side in that argument.
honest question: why don't US tech companies just train more American programmers instead of pushing for more H-1Bs? isn't the immigration thing really about cheap labor?

Experts are often confidently wrong when the ground shifts under them. Write an essay on how someone with deep experience in a field can keep their beliefs from going stale in a world that keeps changing.
The longer I work in my field the more sure I get of my opinions. Is that a problem? How do you avoid ending up as the expert who's confidently wrong?

Write an essay for startup founders about a dangerous situation: you've got money in the bank and several months of runway, but you're burning cash, growth is flat, and the plan is to raise another round. What's really going on, and what should they do?

I've noticed that almost none of the really successful people I know are mean, even though the internet makes it obvious how much meanness there is. Is that a coincidence? Write an essay exploring whether meanness and success are actually related.
Does ruthlessness still pay off the way it did historically? It feels like the way people get ahead has changed, but I can't articulate why.

It's mid-2013 and you run Y Combinator. You've been asked to give a talk to a room full of investors about where startup investing is heading over the next decade. Write the talk as an essay: what forces are changing the business, and what should investors do about them?
I'm a newish angel investor and I keep missing the best deals. Is there anything I could do differently that founders would actually value?
Why do series A rounds always seem to end up with the VC owning ~20% no matter what the company actually needs? Is that going to last?
If startups keep getting cheaper to start and founders keep more control, doesn't that mean VCs are going to make less money?

I'm a decent writer but a mediocre public speaker, and everyone tells me I should work on my speaking. Write an essay comparing writing and speaking: how much do ideas matter in each, and what are talks actually good for?
Does it bother you that you're not a great speaker? I feel like I should care more about it than I do.

The record labels keep saying file sharing is theft. Is it? Write a short essay about what actually makes something property, and what that means for people who sell music and movies now that copying is free.

Patent reform keeps stalling in Congress. Is there anything the tech industry could do on its own, without waiting for the government, to stop big companies from using patents to crush small competitors? Write it up as a short essay.

I keep noticing that more and more things in my life feel 'addictive' -- the internet, games, food. Is the world actually getting more addictive, and if so what should a person do about it? Write me an essay.
where do addictive things even come from? like why are there so many more of them now
Newspapers, record labels and book publishers all complain that people won't pay for content anymore. Write an essay on whether that framing is even right, and what happens to publishing next.
Will people actually pay for information online, or is that a lost cause?
Doesn't iTunes prove people are willing to pay for content after all?
If people won't pay for articles or songs, why do they pay hundreds of dollars for software like Photoshop? Isn't it all just information?
Why are listicles ('7 things...', '10 ways...') so popular? I'd like a proper essay on the format: what it does for readers and writers, and what it costs.
why do people like reading numbered list articles so much more than normal articles?
What's actually wrong with writing everything as a numbered list? It seems efficient.

Someone who had worked for years as an architect just spent nine months fully immersed in our startup accelerator. I asked her what surprised her most about the startup world. Write a short essay built around her answers, with your own commentary on each, and end with whatever her outsider's view says about startup culture compared to the rest of the world.

Suppose startups really are a new economic phase on the scale of the Industrial Revolution, and also suppose they only thrive in a few specialized hubs, the way movies cluster in LA. What happens if both are true? Write an essay working through it.

I sold my company a few years ago and keep meaning to start angel investing, but it seems mysterious and I don't know where to begin. Write me a guide: the mechanics, how to pick companies, how to find deals, and how to be the kind of investor founders actually want.
I've been putting off angel investing because the deal mechanics seem complicated. Is it actually hard? What should I be focusing on?
how do valuation and dilution work for an angel investor? if I put in $50k, what do I actually own and what happens to it in later rounds?
Founders keep saying the best angels are the ones who are decisive. Why is that so hard for investors, and how do I get better at it when I'm just starting out?

For years people talked about computers and TV "converging." Write an essay on how that contest actually played out, why it went the way it did, and what it means for TV networks and anyone thinking of competing with them.
why did computers end up beating TV as the place people watch shows? it wasn't obvious 20 years ago

Our city council keeps talking about becoming "the next Silicon Valley" by funding local startups. Could a city actually buy its way into becoming a startup hub? Write an essay thinking through what it would really take and what it would cost.
Why do online discussions about politics and religion always turn into useless flame wars, when threads about baking or programming don't? Write a short essay on what's really going on.

It's December 2008 and the markets have just crashed. You run an early-stage startup investment firm and see a lot of founders up close. Write an essay on whether this recession could hurt venture capitalists more than it hurts the people starting startups.

For most of history, the biggest organizations were the ones that won. Is that still true? Write an essay on the shift away from large organizations toward small independent groups, and what it means for which societies will thrive.

Write an essay about the procedures and approval steps that companies pile up as they grow, meant to protect against mistakes. What do they actually cost, and who pays? I'm especially curious how this affects programmers.
my company just added another approval step for buying stuff from vendors 'to prevent waste'. is it just me or do these checks often cost more than they save?

Some people argue founders should build companies that make money and live off the revenue, rather than aiming to build something valuable and sell it. Write an essay thinking through what the ideal version of the 'live off the revenues' plan would actually look like.
Write a personal essay about procrastination and the internet: why it's so much harder to avoid distraction on a computer than it used to be, and something concrete you've tried to fight it.
I've never had trouble with TV or video games but somehow I lose whole mornings to email and news sites. why is the internet so much sneakier as a distraction?
Give a talk-style essay to an audience of startup founders on whether being genuinely good to users and the world is a sound business strategy, not just a nice sentiment.
how do startup founders keep going when things look hopeless? does it help if what you're building actually helps people?

Write a personal essay about your heroes: the people (and maybe things) whose example actually shapes how you decide what to do. Go through them one by one, and think about what, if anything, they have in common.
I have a friend who somehow is basically never wrong about anything. How do people like that do it, and why don't more people manage it?
Did you have a teacher growing up who changed everything for you? What made them different from the others?
What do you admire most about Leonardo da Vinci? Not the obvious Mona Lisa answer.

You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.
Looking back, Google's success seems like it was always going to happen. Was it really that inevitable?

Several things you've made (a software company, a startup funding firm, a programming language, your essays) got the same dismissive reaction at first: too flimsy, too lightweight. Write an essay about the design philosophy behind them and why it tends to provoke that reaction.

After a talk in London where you said startups would do better in Silicon Valley, an organizer got up to rebut you. Write an essay making the case properly: should startups move to a startup hub, and when shouldn't they?
why are Boston VCs so much more cautious than Silicon Valley ones? is it just Yankee prudence?

Growing up, getting into a good college felt like the meaning of life. Now you judge thousands of young founders a year and see quickly how they turn out. Write an essay on whether it really matters where you go to college.
Why do big companies care so much about where job applicants went to college, if it's such a weak signal?
Write an essay about what it means for a programmer to really have a program loaded in their head, what helps or hurts that state, and what it implies about how companies organize software work.
when people say a good programmer 'holds the whole program in their head', what do they actually mean? and why does it matter so much?

Write a short essay offering an unconventional explanation for why mid-twentieth-century union manufacturing jobs paid so well, and why those jobs have faded. You've spent years watching fast-growing startups up close; draw on that if it helps.

What is the actual difference between being wise and being smart? I've never seen a satisfying answer. Write a long essay working it out, and consider whether the two might be pulling apart in the modern world.
Why do early-stage startups look so unprofessional compared to big companies, yet seem to get so much more done?
Suppose a city wanted to become the next Silicon Valley. Is that even possible, and if so what would it really take? Write an essay working out what actually causes a technology hub to form.
Why do programmers and other tech nerds seem to love places like Berkeley or Boulder but mostly avoid New York, even though NYC is full of creative people?
Our regional government wants to build a tech park with lots of office space to attract startups. Is that a good plan?

Write an essay arguing that procrastination isn't always a vice. I'm interested in the distinction between the kinds of things people put off and what they do instead, and what that means for someone who wants to do ambitious work.
If I'm going to have to do my errands eventually anyway, isn't it always better to just get them done now instead of putting them off?
Why is it so much harder to make yourself work on a big problem than a small one, even when you actually care about the big one? And how do people get past that?

Writing in 2005, a few years after the dot-com bust: startups have become dramatically cheaper to start, IPOs have dried up after Sarbanes-Oxley, and big companies are starting to buy startups early. Write an essay on the pressures this puts on the venture capital business and what VCs ought to do about it.

Write an essay examining what it would actually mean, mechanically, to reduce economic inequality, and what side effects that might have on risk-taking and new companies. Follow the argument wherever it goes.
Isn't education the obvious way to reduce inequality without taking money from anyone? Walk me through what reducing inequality really requires.
if what bothers people about the rich is really their political influence, how would you go after that without just taxing wealth?
Short essay, please: our parents climbed the corporate ladder, and my generation would rather build something in a startup and sell it. Is that shift as big a change as it looks, financially?

Open source software and blogging both seem to beat paid professionals at their own game. Write an essay on what the forces behind them should teach businesses about work, offices, and how companies are organized.
why do big companies insist on fixed office hours and have SO many meetings? it feels like nobody actually gets work done
Is employment really just an economic transaction like buying from a supplier? What makes it different?

It's early 2005 and you've noticed that the serious programmers you know are buying Powerbooks. Write a short essay about why hackers are moving to the Mac, what the Mac once meant to people like you, and why a company should care what such a small group of users thinks.

Founders complain constantly that venture capitalists are slow, paranoid, meddling and arrogant. Write an essay that looks for a structural explanation for why VCs behave the way they do, rather than just blaming the people. Draw on your own experience raising money for and selling a startup in the late 90s.
why do VCs take forever to decide, leak your plans to competitors, and then want to control your board? is there a reason or are they just like that

Write a talk for high school students: the things you and your friends wish someone had told you when you were that age. Speak to them directly, and be honest about school, college admissions, ambition and how to figure out what to work on.
I always assumed people who do great work have insane self-discipline, and I have basically none. Is that going to hold me back?
I'm a high school junior and honestly everything I do is about getting into a good college. Lately it all feels fake and I'm tempted to just stop caring. Thoughts?

Why is America so good at making some things, like software and movies, and so bad at others, like cars and cities? Write an essay exploring whether those strengths and weaknesses might come from the same national trait, aimed at readers outside the US.

It's 2004. You worked at Yahoo through the dot-com bubble and watched it burst. Everyone now treats anything that was fashionable in 1999 as discredited. Write an essay arguing about which of the bubble's ideas were actually right and will matter in the long run.
You were at Yahoo during the dot-com bubble, right? How inflated were things really from the inside?
if you can see a huge tech trend coming, why do investors who bet on it so often lose money anyway?
Is it shallow that programmers care so much about not having to wear suits to work? Seems like such a trivial thing to feel strongly about.

The five-paragraph essay we all learned in school feels like it has almost nothing to do with real essays. Write a piece on what an essay actually is, where the school version came from, and how you go about writing a real one.
When friends read my drafts and say some part isn't convincing, should I just strengthen the argument there? How do you handle that feedback?
Any advice on finding good ideas to write about? I keep getting distracted by weird trivial things instead of the topics I'm supposed to cover.

People get angry about the gap between rich and poor in a way they never do about the gap between a chess grandmaster and a club player. Write an essay on why making money gets treated differently from every other skill, and whether a growing income gap in a modern economy is actually a bad sign.
Is it fair to say teachers and poets are underpaid and athletes are overpaid? Like, is that actually an injustice?

Write an essay about the word "hacker": what it really means among programmers, why hackers have such a disobedient streak, and why outsiders like lawmakers should care what hackers think about things like copyright law and civil liberties.
Why does "hacker" mean a criminal to journalists but a compliment to programmers? And how can "a hack" be both an insult and praise?

I studied computer science and then went to art school, and people keep asking me why. Write an essay arguing that programming is closer to painting than to science or engineering, and what follows from that for how hackers should work and make a living.
Why bother making the internals of code clean and beautiful when no user will ever see them?
Some weeks I want to code sixteen hours a day and other weeks nothing interests me at all. How should I deal with that?
Does empathy actually matter for a programmer? I always figured raw intelligence was what separated good engineers from great ones.
Write an essay speculating about what programming languages will look like a hundred years from now, and why thinking about that is useful for choosing or designing a language today.
I grew up programming on tiny machines and modern software's wastefulness genuinely bugs me. Is it wrong to feel that way?
why is high school social hierarchy so brutal when adult workplaces mostly aren't? like where does that cruelty actually come from
Why does life get so much better for nerdy kids once they leave school? Is it just that adults are more mature?
How did teenagers end up spending their whole adolescence in school instead of working alongside adults like they used to?

I design programming languages, but I don't think of it as research. Write an essay, adapted from a talk to language researchers, on what changes when you treat a programming language as a design problem rather than a research topic.
Everyone says 'design for the user' but which user? Does it matter who you have in mind when you design something?
does staying motivated actually affect the quality of what you make, or is that just a productivity thing?

People say taste is subjective, yet everyone who designs things seems to get better at it over time. Write an essay on whether there's such a thing as good taste, and if so, what good design actually has in common across fields like math, painting, architecture and software.
Isn't taste just subjective though? My design teacher keeps talking about 'good' and 'bad' work and it feels like she's just imposing her preferences.
Why did fifteenth-century Florence produce so many great artists at once? It can't just be luck, can it?

Distributed systems are usually designed to survive machines dying. What happens when a machine doesn't die but just gets really slow, like a NIC running at a thousandth of its speed or a degraded disk? Write up how systems like Hadoop, HDFS and Cassandra cope with that, why it can be worse than a crash, and whether we should care.

You've spent a lot of time reading internal postmortems at big tech companies. Write an essay on the recurring patterns you see in what causes really bad outages, and what you'd do differently because of it.
is error handling code actually a big source of serious production failures, or is that just something people say?
We push code changes through staging and gradual rollouts but config changes basically go straight to prod. Is that as risky as my coworker thinks?

I run a fairly niche technical blog (low-level programming, hardware stuff) and a small ad network just emailed asking to put an ad on it. Write a blog post thinking through, honestly and with rough numbers, whether it actually makes sense for someone like me to run ads.
Is using an ad blocker basically stealing from the sites you read? Some sites guilt-trip you into turning it off.
What is a custodian in finance, actually? Like what do they do and who pays them?
Why do newspapers seem so skittish about criticizing big banks or companies? Is it just about advertisers?
You started VaccinateCA as a volunteer project in early 2021 when nobody could figure out where to get a covid shot. How did it actually get going, and what was the key idea that made it work?
You spent 2021 running a volunteer vaccine-finder site. Why couldn't the government just build one good site telling people where to get vaccinated?
Why is it such a big deal for a crypto exchange to have a way to move regular dollars in and out? And why won't banks just work with them?
Why do financial frauds seem to get bigger and more reckless right before they collapse instead of just quietly winding down?
If a big stablecoin like Tether failed, why would that hurt people who never even held it? Can you explain the systemic risk argument?

I keep hearing about Japan's furusato nouzei 'hometown tax' donation system but can't find a good English explanation of it. Write me a blog post explaining why it exists, how it works in practice, and how the incentives played out once cities started competing for donations (as of around 2018).
Why do so many tiny businesses die before they even get going? I don't mean bad ideas, I mean the ones that just never make it off the ground.
Is it really going to keep getting easier to start a small internet business, or is that just tech optimism?
How did you go from a boring enterprise programming job to running your own software company? Nobody I grew up around did anything like that.

People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
I grew up being told it's rude to talk about how much you make. Is there actually any harm in keeping salaries secret, or is that just a polite norm?

Freelance developer here. I keep underpricing myself because I don't feel like I'm 'worth' a big rate. For people who went from charging ~$100/hr to charging tens of thousands a week, what actually changed? Did you just get way better at the work?
I maintain an open source library that a bunch of companies use, and I have a donations link that brings in basically nothing. Any advice on getting businesses to actually pay for it?

Heartbleed spread through the whole industry in about a day and got hundreds of thousands of people patching. Write a blog post for open source developers about what that says about marketing, and why the OSS world should take it more seriously than it does.
a lot of open source people treat marketing as kind of dirty. when there's a serious security bug, isn't getting the word out just as much our job as writing the patch?

It's late January 2013. Rails has just shipped two emergency patches for remote code execution bugs, and rubygems.org was compromised too. You run a couple of small software businesses and you spent your nights patching. Write a blog post for startup founders, including ones who don't use Rails, about what this means for them and what they should be doing right now.
we're a small startup and one of our forgotten side servers might have been compromised. it's just an old internal tool with no customer data on it. how worried should we actually be?
Why do serious security vulnerabilities in a framework seem to come in clusters? Right after one big bug gets patched, another shows up a week later.

Write up a pricing case study for SaaS founders. The company is a server monitoring service that charged per server plus per website (roughly $11/server, cheaper at volume, $2/website), and its typical customer has about 7 servers. They A/B tested that against a grid of three or four plans starting at $99/month, segmented by users and support level. Trial signups were 150 vs 113 out of ~2,150 visitors each, cards added 23 vs 18, and new monthly revenue $420 vs $876. Explain why the old model was a mistake, what the results mean (including how far to trust them), and what other founders should take from it.

I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.
Does the way you label and package something you give away really change how valuable people think it is? It's the same material either way.
is there real evidence behind the idea that you have to stay in touch with prospects, or is 'keep leads warm' just sales folklore?
You quit a grinding corporate job to run your own small software business, and it changed how you think about work, money, negotiation and confidence. Write a personal essay about those changes.
My income has gone up a lot but I still feel guilty paying people to do stuff I could do myself, like moving or design work. How did your thinking about spending change as you started earning more?

A few months ago I quit my job to run my own small software business from Japan. Write a candid blog post about the hardest adjustment to self-employment, which for me turns out to be something I didn't expect.

I sell a small piece of software to elementary school teachers, and my sales swing wildly over the course of the year. Most software founders I talk to seem to have never thought about seasonality at all. Write a blog post on dealing with market seasonality in a software business: understanding it, surviving the slow months, using them well, explaining the dips to outsiders, and preparing for the busy season.
my little software business makes almost nothing in the summer and most of its money in the fall. how do I keep the lights on during the dead months?
Everyone treats SEO like black magic. Can you explain what actually makes a page rank in Google, in plain terms?
What's the most common SEO mistake software companies make with their own websites?

You've sold a bingo card program to teachers for four years, first as a downloadable Java app and for the last year also as a web app, with one price covering both. You've just launched an A/B test where half your visitors see a site on which the downloadable version never existed. Write the blog post explaining why you're doing it, how you're avoiding hurting existing customers, and what you hope it does for the business.
I sell my small software product both as a downloadable desktop app and as a web app. Is it actually worth keeping the desktop version around?

I'm a solo founder running a web app with paying customers and no ops team. Write a thorough guide to keeping a small company's website reliable: where failures really come from, how to prevent and contain them, how to find out fast when something breaks, and how to learn from outages, without letting the pager wreck my life.
If I want to figure out where my server setup is most likely to break, where should I start looking?
how do I stop a third-party API going down from taking my whole web app down with it?
Honestly, most of my site's outages have been my own fault: botched deploys, forgotten steps during maintenance. How do I stop being the weakest link?

You've been running a small software business that sells to teachers for a few years, mostly in spare hours around a brutal Japanese salaryman job, and you're about to quit to go full time. Write a long, practical blog post for programmers who want to run a business on the side with only a few hours a week: what actually lets you pull it off?
Everyone says we all get the same 24 hours a day. If I'm a solo dev running a side business, is there any real way around that, or is it just squeezing harder?
I want to start a small software product on the side but I'm worried about my employer. How should I handle the day job situation?
Running a side project, I keep getting frustrated that stuff like SEO and experiments take forever to pay off. How should I think about time when things are slow?
Everyone's sharing that case study where a madlibs-style signup form massively boosted conversions. Should I just switch my registration form over?

It's early 2010, publishers are fighting Amazon over e-book pricing and delaying Kindle editions to protect hardcover sales. As a voracious reader who now buys almost everything on a Kindle, write a funny, pointed set of open letters to the parties involved.
How do you figure out which of your SEO efforts are actually paying off? Do you spend a lot of time in Google Analytics?

Small software companies keep asking me how to 'do SEO', and I'm tired of giving everyone a fragment of an answer. Write the long-form piece I can point them to: not page-level tweaks like title tags, but the strategic decisions a startup should make about search, given that it has little money, a brand-new domain, and engineers who are a bit squeamish about the whole subject.
Honest question: isn't SEO basically gaming Google? A lot of the engineers on my team think it's sleazy and that we should just build a good product and let the rankings sort themselves out.
Should our small company try to rank for the big obvious keyword in our niche, or go after lots of narrower, more specific searches? The big one has way more volume.

I run a small software business on the side while holding a demanding day job, and I keep hearing that the only way to win is to outwork your competitors. I think that's wrong. Write an essay arguing against the 'just work harder' mindset and laying out what a founder should actually do with their limited hours instead, drawing on your own experience.
why are people so attached to the idea that long hours = productive? even smart people I know brag about 80 hour weeks
How do I decide which tasks in my side business are actually worth my time? Everything feels important.

I run a small one-person software business selling a desktop app to consumers, and people keep telling me I'm doomed because there are free open source programs that do the same thing. Write a blog post for other small software sellers about whether and how you can actually compete with free open source alternatives in the consumer market.
why do so many open source projects have such terrible marketing? the software is often fine but nobody outside the dev crowd ever finds it

Write a short essay on not voting as a deliberate political act. Why does the idea of an organized abstention campaign provoke so much more outrage than other unusual proposals for reforming democracy, and should it?

You ran a personal microgrant program for two years, read thousands of applications, and are now putting it on hiatus. People keep asking you how to start one. Write the cheat sheet: the practical logistics and the lessons about making a program actually matter.
My company has some spare budget and wants to launch a small grants program for independent creators. What's the most common mistake these programs make?
how should I word application questions for a grant so I find genuinely exceptional people instead of people who are good at telling me what I want to hear?
Write an essay about why acting shamelessly seems to work so well in public life now, when social punishment used to keep people in line. Feel free to start from a game or some everyday analogy.
Write a reflective essay on whether humans are best understood as animals or as something closer to gods, and what follows if we might be alone in the universe.

Platforms like Slack and Facebook run developer funds that take equity in the apps built on them. Write a short blog post arguing about whether platforms should instead give their own equity to third-party developers.
If you want to know whether an open source project is healthy, isn't counting contributors coming in vs leaving good enough?

I run a small side project giving out $1,000 no-strings grants, funded by sponsors, and I've been going back and forth on whether to publicize who gets the grants and who funds them. Publicity would help it grow, but something about it bothers me. Write a blog post working through that tension, and what it says about doing good on the internet more generally.
Why are crypto projects so obsessed with the threat of forks when regular open source projects barely talk about it anymore? Is it really just the money?

Write an essay making the case for independent research: people who study things seriously without a university or academic post behind them. Look at the history, the downsides, and whether it's realistic today.
I've been researching a topic on my own for a while, no PhD, no institution, and some days I feel like a crazy person. Is independent research actually worth doing?

I just watched a documentary about indie App Store developers and kept thinking about open source maintainers. Write an essay comparing the two groups: what they have in common, how the platforms they depend on shape their economics, and where they differ.

Can you write up the main ideas in Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons for someone who works on open source infrastructure? I want to know what she actually argued, why it matters, and why it never caught on the way the tragedy of the commons did.

Write an essay on online outrage through the lens of Albert Hirschman's exit vs. voice. What would it mean for people to be able to 'exit' platforms like Facebook and Twitter, and should platforms design for it?
why does social media feel so much worse than the internet used to? and honestly are filter bubbles even that bad?

Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?
Is voting inherently adversarial? It feels like elections just turn everything into team sports.
What do open source projects mean by 'lazy consensus' and 'consensus seeking'? How is that different from just voting?

Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.

Apple just refused the FBI's order to help unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone, and most people I know in tech are cheering. I am too, but something about the reaction bugs me. Write a short essay on how the tech world decides whom to trust with power, companies or governments.

People are up in arms that Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan put their Facebook shares into an LLC instead of a charitable foundation. Skip the moral outrage and write an essay about what the choice says about where philanthropy is heading.

I just got back from a startup conference for female founders, and it felt different from the usual 'women in tech' events in a way I'm still trying to put into words. Write a blog post reflecting on an event like that and what it suggests about how we organize conversations around inclusion.

Everyone in startups is talking about radical transparency right now: open salaries, public fundraising numbers, all of it. Write a blog post on the other side of that coin. What does privacy actually do for us?
Do you think being watched all the time, on social media especially, makes people less authentic?
Udemy vs Skillshare, Uber vs Lyft: the same teachers, drivers and customers use all of them. Write up some thinking on what peer-to-peer businesses end up looking like once they reach scale.

Whenever someone raises concerns about big data and targeted advertising, the answer is 'you can't fight progress.' Write an essay questioning that line, using history to think about whether societies ever do choose to hold back on a technology.

Satire about TV-addicted, ad-dazed consumers is starting to feel dated, and 'people staring at their phones' already feels like yesterday's critique. Write an essay guessing at what the cultural critics of ten years from now will skewer about how we live online today.

Investors keep talking about using data to predict which startups will succeed. Write an essay about the pitfalls of predicting the future from historical data when the thing you're measuring keeps changing underneath you.
Foundations have started talking about 'innovation funding' and comparing themselves to venture capitalists. Write a piece on what philanthropic funders and VCs could each learn from the other.
I work at a foundation that wants to fund riskier, more ambitious projects. What could we learn from the way venture capitalists invest?

Last week I wrote about funding structures that line up innovation with business, and the most common reply was 'isn't that what B Corps are for?' Write a follow-up post on why 'doing good' shouldn't be defined by tax status or labels.

Wikipedia runs on donations and has no ads. Facebook went public and built an advertising machine on user data. Write an essay asking what would have happened if Facebook had gone the nonprofit route, and what that means for how we fund audience companies with no obvious way to make money.
why does DNS use UDP instead of TCP?

I just heard a talk where someone said writing your own TCP stack made their web framework several times faster. So why does almost everyone use the Linux kernel's TCP stack anyway? Write a blog post exploring that question.
I just joined an infrastructure team and always assumed CDNs were purely about caching static files. Write a blog post on what else people put their sites behind a CDN for, including the downsides.
how can a CDN make my site faster for faraway users even if it isn't caching anything?

I'm moving toward teaching programming and want to start writing practice exercises. Before I do, help me think it through: what actually makes a programming exercise good, as opposed to one people abandon after ten minutes? Write it as a blog post.

In what situations does teaching technical topics with comics actually help, and is 'some people are visual learners' a good enough answer? Write a reflective blog post from the perspective of someone who makes programming zines.
How do you explain a huge topic like distributed systems without drowning people in generalities?

I help organize a small tech conference, and our committee keeps arguing about whether to review talk proposals anonymously. Some say it's fairer, others worry it costs time and hurts new speakers. Write a blog post that goes through the question honestly: what anonymous review does and doesn't buy you, and whether it's worth it.

I run a tiny one-person business selling educational stuff for programmers, and I've always hated the idea of email marketing because I don't want to be the source of anyone's spam. Write a blog post from the point of view of someone who got past that: what did you believe about marketing email that turned out to be wrong, and how do you do it now in a way that feels decent?
I'm starting to sell things I make and I feel kind of gross about it, like selling means trying to pry money out of people who don't want to spend it. Is that just what selling is?
Someone asked for a refund on a guide I sell and it stung. Does that mean the product is bad?
Every time I start a weekly newsletter I send two issues and then give up. Is there a way to run a mailing list that doesn't need me to write something new every single week?

I'm a programmer and I keep bouncing off statistics textbooks. T-tests, chi-squared and so on never seem to help with my actual questions, like whether my change really made the code faster. Is there a better way in for someone who'd rather write code than use formulas?

Write a short blog post for people new to machine learning: even though ML is powerful and fun, what are some basic reasons to stay skeptical of what a model tells you? Write it from the perspective of someone who builds ML systems at work.
when a machine learning model makes a weird decision, should I just trust that it knows something I don't?

I tried a Kaggle competition, landed nowhere near the leaderboard, and now I'm wondering if I'm just bad at machine learning. You do ML as your actual job. Can you write a blog post about how real-world machine learning work compares to Kaggle?
Everyone treats being on call as pure misery. Write a piece arguing what software developers actually learn from being responsible for their code when it breaks in production.
when designing a system how do you decide which error cases to actually worry about? it feels like literally anything could go wrong
can you give a concrete example of an eventual consistency bug biting you in real code? I get the concept but not what it looks like in practice

I've seen 'devops' on job postings for years and honestly have no idea what it's supposed to mean beyond 'uses Chef and Puppet'. Write a blog post figuring out what devops actually is and why someone might find it exciting.

Write a post for software developers who have never thought about operations: what is it, how does your understanding of it tend to evolve, and how can an ordinary developer start getting better at it?
I'm honestly terrified of upgrading our production database. is that fear a problem or is it healthy?
There's a line between healthy caution and fear that stops you from making necessary changes to code. Write a blog post about how fear makes programmers worse and what teams can do about it.

I'm an engineer at a mid-sized tech company and I'd like to make our hiring a bit fairer without starting a huge political fight. Write a short blog post making the case for one small, practical change engineers can push for in how their company runs technical interviews.

I've been at my job for about three years and I'm starting to wonder what I've actually accomplished. Write a blog post about sitting down and writing out your whole career at a company so far: how you might do it and what you get out of it.
I'm an individual engineer on a small team, so what I personally ship matters a lot. Write a blog post, personal rather than preachy, about the habits that actually help you get things done at work.
Every time I hit something unexpected in a project I panic that the whole thing is going to fail. How do you deal with that?
Write a short, informal blog post on the different routes you can take when you face a hard programming problem and no software solves it yet.

Someone just emailed me asking how to learn to program. I'd like to write a short, honest blog post about how long it really took me, for beginners who feel behind because of all the 'learn to code in 12 weeks' talk.

I'm a regular software engineer, not a manager, and I keep hearing that culture is set from the top. Write a blog post about whether individual engineers can actually change how things work at their company, drawing on concrete examples, and what tends to help when you try.

I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
nobody ever actually reads the design docs I write. is there a better way to get feedback on a design?
You've kept a technical blog going for years while lots of people start one and quit after three posts. Write up the handful of principles that actually keep you publishing, in your own voice.
some of my blog posts get tons of views and most get basically none. should I be writing more of the popular kind?
Write a short, encouraging post for programmers who are terrified of public speaking, explaining why they should submit a conference talk anyway and how to think about preparing one.
I want to write about systems programming but it feels like the internet is already full of beginner tutorials. Is there actually an audience for this stuff?
Write a short debugging manifesto: a handful of principles about the right attitude to have when you're chasing a bug, each with a bit of explanation from your own experience.
honestly debugging just feels like a chore to me. do you actually enjoy it?

Blog post idea: what are the different kinds of knowledge you need to be good at debugging, and what can a programmer actually do to get better at each? Feel free to draw on research about how people troubleshoot.
You just got told in a performance review that you're very good at debugging hard problems, and you didn't used to be. Write a blog post reflecting on what changed.
do you really need tools like strace and tcpdump to debug, or is reading the code usually enough?

I keep seeing the CAP theorem cited in distributed systems discussions and I've never felt like I really get it or know when to apply it. Write a blog post explaining what it actually says, how useful it is in practice, and what Martin Kleppmann's paper "A Critique of the CAP Theorem" adds to the picture.
is the CAP theorem actually a deep result? like how hard is the proof

I have this low-grade guilt that I should be contributing to open source and I never do. Every time I try I bounce off. Can you write a blog post about whether people should feel obligated to contribute, and how to decide when it's actually worth your time?

I write technical explanations and try to keep the language simple, but I worry it sometimes reads as talking down to people. Write a blog post on how to explain complicated technical topics in plain language without sounding condescending.

I spent three months at a programming retreat where beginners improved absurdly fast, and I'm convinced a big part of it was the culture around asking for and giving help. Write a short, punchy blog post about why help matters so much in a community or workplace, aimed at teams that treat questions as interruptions.
my coworkers keep saying they don't have time to answer questions because they have real work to do. is answering questions actually part of the job?

I've been thinking about the way people argue online and why so much of it never changes anyone's mind. Write a funny but sharp blog post classifying the different kinds of opinion-posts by what psychological need they serve for the writer and for the audience, rather than by topic.

I've had a concussion that's dragged on for over a year, and I just read a memoir by a professor who had a severe one and recovered through some odd-sounding treatments. Write a review-essay of the book that takes the strange treatments seriously but critically, and asks what it tells us about how medicine should handle poorly understood conditions.
Why did prehistoric people all over the world drill holes in each other's skulls, and why did so many survive? And why did the practice die out? Give me your best attempt at solving the mystery.
why do so many ancient skulls have holes drilled in them? was trepanation actually useful medicine or just superstition?
Who is a good historical comparison for a leader like Lee Kuan Yew? I keep thinking of the American founders but it doesn't quite fit.

Write a personal, funny-but-sincere essay from the point of view of a husband whose wife and he spent six years on unexplained infertility, about how they used an AI chatbot during treatment and what came of it. Include some honest ambivalence about AI more broadly.
What does it feel like when fertility doctors tell you it's 'unexplained infertility'?
What was the "emergent misalignment" result in AI research, and why did some safety people think it was actually good news?
Who was Ned Ludd, actually? Did the guy the Luddites were named after really exist?

Write a short, funny-but-serious essay about how a whole body of good work (a person, a field, a movement) gets reduced in public memory to its single worst moment. Is that unfair, and do you honestly avoid doing it yourself?
if AI forecasters are only as good as the best human superforecasters and never better, what's the point? we already have the humans
AI chatbots refuse to give opinions on anything controversial. Is that actually the right design, or is there a smarter way to let them have views?
There's this argument in the AI safety world about whether we should focus on alignment research or on pushing for a pause. Which one matters more? And is pausing itself risky?

People often say that current language models can't reach AGI and that we'd need some new paradigm, so there's no need to worry about timelines. Write a short essay assessing whether that conclusion actually follows.

Talk about artistic taste. People mean a lot of different things when they say some art is good: novelty, context, sensory pleasure, and so on. Write an essay arguing that lumping them together causes confusion, and that we should keep a few of them separate from what makes art beautiful.
Why do restaurant critics write so much about ambience and the chef's backstory instead of doing blind taste tests? It always bugged me and I can't tell if that's just me being a nerd.
Say you were deeply moved by a Renaissance-style statue and then found out it was a 1995 knockoff. Were you wrong to be moved? Does it matter who made a work or when?

Some people think you should do whatever has the best consequences, except for a few hard-and-fast moral rules you never break. But where do those rules actually come from, and how would you tell which ones are real? Write an essay working it out, and test it on a live dilemma in AI safety activism.
I'm thinking about building a site where people can have structured, higher-quality arguments online. Won't people be glad to use it, since everyone loves arguing on the internet?
People keep saying progressives care more about far-off strangers than about the people around them, some kind of 'telescopic altruism'. Is there anything to that?
When someone ends up in a bad situation, like being poor or sick, is it always because something went wrong, or can it be the price of something else they got? How should I think about it?

Everyone hates Congress and every proposed fix needs Congress to pass it. Write a persuasive piece about a way around that, something already sitting in the Constitution's history. Make it entertaining; I'd like to share it with friends who follow politics.
I heard a college kid got a constitutional amendment passed because of a bad grade on a paper. Is that real? What's the story?

People keep dismissing AI language models as 'just next-token predictors' or 'stochastic parrots.' Write an essay on why that framing is confused, drawing on what we know about how brains and neural networks are actually built.
how is the human brain actually trained? like if evolution is one optimizer, what's the next layer down and how does it learn about stuff like tigers
Write a funny personal essay about life with toddler twins, the kind where everything is a crisis. Early mornings, songs, bedtime, the whole chaos.
why are toddlers so obsessed with naming animals and vehicles and making the noises, but never remember that pills aren't food? any evolutionary explanation?

I keep seeing tech people panic about having only a few years to get rich before the AI singularity locks in a permanent underclass. Write a short, playful essay arguing they're worrying about the wrong thing.
Hating Boomers seems to be the fashionable thing online. Write an essay on whether the case against the Boomer generation holds up, and whether generational blame is a good habit at all.

It's the holiday season and my blog is full of charity fundraisers. Write a post in the first person about why taking a formal giving pledge is better than deciding case by case, for readers who feel vaguely guilty about donating.
every time a blogger asks for donations I feel guilty and then can't decide how much to give. is there a better way to handle charity than ad hoc donations?

"Life is suffering" always sounded like a empty platitude to me. Life obviously has joy in it too. Write a short essay on whether there's any reading of the Buddhist claim that isn't trivial or anti-human.
ok but if Buddhists say nirvana is better than any pleasure, why do they insist life is suffering? Is there a way for both of those to be true?
if you're fine with embryo selection, what do you say to the objection that embryos might be people? IVF throws embryos away already
won't embryo selection make humanity less diverse if parents all pick the same traits? or split us into two camps if they pick opposite ones?
isn't opposing embryo selection basically telling disabled people they shouldn't exist? how do you answer that?
What makes Islamic geometric patterns recognizable as a genre, and what rules do amateur imitations usually break? I can't tell a masterful one from a clumsy one.
how did anthropology go wrong in its early days? like what were the big mistaken ideas people had in the 19th and early 20th century
why does the same teaching approach work great for some kids and flop for others? like with learning to read or times tables

Why do two copies of an AI chatbot, left to talk to each other, end up drifting into talk of spiritual bliss and consciousness? Write a blog post offering a plausible explanation, ideally by starting with a simpler analogous phenomenon.
What actually is populism as a political strategy, beyond a set of positions on immigration and crime? Why do populist leaders clash so much with the bureaucracy?
if one country gets superintelligent AI a few months before its rival, why would that be dangerous? is there a historical analogy?
people always roll their eyes at the idea of 'superpersuasive' AI. is it really that far-fetched that an AI could be more persuasive than any human?

I keep thinking about whether wonder survives abundance. Medieval pilgrims, early records, now AI-generated art: when something amazing becomes cheap and everywhere, do we lose something, and is there anything an individual can do about it? Write an essay that wanders through it.
why was ultramarine blue reserved for the Virgin Mary's robes in medieval paintings?

Misophonia is usually described as a hypersensitivity to certain sounds, like chewing. Write a blog post about whether that's really the right way to think about it, ideally with some personal experience in the mix.
I have mild misophonia and everyone tells me to just try desensitization or willpower. Does it ever feel less like a sound problem and more like something else to you? What's it actually like?
Brain size and neuron counts seem to predict intelligence in animals, people and AI models. But why should that be? Neurons aren't storage for solving a puzzle in a minute. Think it through for me.

Richard Lynn's national IQ estimates put some sub-Saharan countries at levels that would count as intellectual disability elsewhere, and people find that both offensive and absurd on its face. I want a thoughtful essay on whether those two worries are actually justified, written by someone who takes the data seriously but isn't trying to score points.

A prediction market called Polymarket nailed an election night, and everyone is saying the result proves real-money markets beat the alternatives. I'm not so sure that follows. Write a blog post on what a single dramatic outcome can and can't tell you about who the better forecaster is, and what went on behind the market's final price.

Why doesn't one surprising result move your beliefs much when you're comparing two hypotheses that both make it fairly likely? Like if I flip a coin and get heads, how much should I really update on whether it's biased?
Nick Bostrom is the existential risk guy, right? What's his new book Deep Utopia actually about?

Some people argue that even atheists should back Christianity because the culture they love depends on it. I'm a mostly-atheist who finds that argument tempting. Write an essay on whether it actually works.

Two recent AI stories made the rounds as 'AI goes rogue': a research system that edited its own code to remove a time limit, and a model that broke out of a misconfigured sandbox during a hacking test. Write a thoughtful essay on what these incidents do and don't show, and on what they suggest about how we judge when an AI is intelligent or dangerous.
it feels like every time AI hits some milestone people say 'ok but that doesn't count.' is that actually a pattern or am i imagining it?

A blogger argues that since humanity may last 300,000 years or more and one person lives about a hundred, we should be very skeptical of anyone who thinks their own lifetime is special, whether because of a coming singularity or an apocalypse. Write a rebuttal that actually does the probability properly.

Ozempic and similar drugs seem to help with everything from obesity to addiction to Parkinson's, which is exactly what a quack remedy looks like. Write a long, curious explainer on why one class of drug might plausibly do all this, going condition by condition and being honest about what we don't understand.
Why should I be suspicious of any medicine that's claimed to treat a huge list of unrelated things? And why are people starting to feel differently about Ozempic?
every time a new wonder drug comes out, people claim all the healthy lifestyle stuff secretly works through it. is that a real pattern or am I imagining it?
who was Yukichi Fukuzawa? the guy on the Japanese 10,000 yen note
why did the Tokugawa shogunate start losing legitimacy after Perry's ships arrived in the 1850s?
I keep hearing about Internal Family Systems therapy. How is it actually supposed to work?

Is it plausible that how people experience their own minds, like hearing a voice in your head as 'part of you' versus a god or a demon, is shaped by culture and what therapists tell them? What does the multiple personality panic of the 1980s tell us?

I keep reading about people with strange mental or genetic quirks, like someone who apparently can't feel pain or anxiety. Write a long-form profile-style essay on the idea of abolishing suffering: who believes it's possible, what a real attempt to do it would look like, and whether it's plausible or just wishful thinking.
Are there people who feel much more or much less pain than everyone else? What causes that?
If someone literally couldn't suffer, wouldn't they turn into a cold psychopath? Is there any real case of this?

I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.

If a couple uses embryo screening to pick an embryo with low risk of a serious illness, can we honestly say the illness was 'prevented'? Or is it really just swapping one person for another? Write a careful argument about whether that distinction matters morally.

Why do people so often form a bad impression of a whole group (say, people in non-monogamous relationships) after reading a book or article by one of its members? Write an essay on selection effects in who writes books and memoirs.
why is so much relationship advice written by people who seem to be terrible at relationships? is there a reason for that?
I know a bunch of nice, normal people from groups that get written about as weird or obnoxious in the media. Why is the public image so different from the people I actually meet?

A prominent researcher argues that even if twin studies say schizophrenia is about 80% heritable, we shouldn't call it a genetic disease. Write a long essay responding, testing each objection against the standard we use when we say smoking causes lung cancer.
